text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft this, a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter can say.

1. **Who is it addressed to, and is there a deadline or form?** Is it a named admissions officer or "Admissions Committee"? Some programs ask referees specific questions, and the letter should answer those directly. I also need your name, the farm's name, and the contact details you want under your signature.

2. **The weaker written English.** The committee will see his writing in the application anyway, so the letter should deal with it rather than leave it out. How does he handle written work on the job now? For example, does he enter notes in the herd software or keep milking logs? What is the night class, and how long has he been taking it? Any progress you've noticed would help.

3. **The 5 weeks away last summer.** I'd suggest one honest sentence: a family emergency, and he came back. That fits with 2 missed shifts in 3 years, and it's better than the committee hearing about it some other way. A few details would make that sentence stronger. Did he come back when he said he would? Did he help arrange cover before he left? Did you hold his job? Do you want it in the letter at all?

4. **The 9 mastitis cases.** Do you know what catching them early meant in practice? That could be treatment cost saved, cows kept in the milking string, or anything the vet said about it. A rough figure you'd stand behind is fine.

5. **The software.** Did he teach himself? Does he now show other workers how to use it, or did he take on the sick-cow flagging on his own initiative?

6. **After the program.** Would you rehire him or keep a place for him? Are you adjusting his hours so he can study? This is the strongest backing a farm manager can give an agricultural program, so only include what you'd actually commit to.

If you don't know some of these, say so and I'll write the letter without them. I won't fill gaps with guesses.

1. I don't have a name, so "Admissions Committee" is fine. It's due February 1 through the college's online portal. I don't know of any specific questions they want answered. I'm Mike Hollis, farm manager at Hollis Dairy. My phone is 555-0187, and I'm fine with the committee calling me.

2. I don't know the details of the night class or how long he's been in it. I don't know how much he writes in the software either. He did fail the written test in a dairy safety course once and passed it the second time.

3. Yes, put it in. Before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would.

4. The vet said catching those cases early saved us about $8,000.

5. I don't know.

6. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program.

I've drafted the letter. I included every fact you gave, including the two days' notice and the failed safety test. The committee will see his written English in his application anyway, so the letter brings it up first and answers it with the night class and the retake he passed.

<final_document>
Admissions Committee
Agricultural Technology Program

Dear Admissions Committee,

I am the farm manager at Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow dairy. I am writing to recommend Tomás for your two-year agricultural technology program. He has worked for us for three years, since he was 19, and I recommend him without reservation.

Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift by himself, five days a week. No one else is on the farm at that hour to check his work or cover for him. In three years he has missed two shifts.

He has also become the person who gets the most out of our herd management software. He learned the system and now uses it to flag sick cows for our vet. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early, and our vet estimates that this saved the farm about $8,000. Your program trains people to use data to manage animal health, and Tomás is already doing that work.

You should know about one absence. Last summer his father fell ill in Mexico, and Tomás was away for five weeks. He told me two days before he left, which was short notice. Before he went, though, he arranged for his cousin, a former employee of ours, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. I count that as evidence of his reliability.

His spoken English is stronger than his written English. He knows this and is taking a night class to improve it. He failed the written test in a dairy safety course the first time and passed it on his second attempt. I expect the written coursework to take him more effort than the hands-on work. I also expect him to put that effort in, because that is how he has handled everything we have asked of him.

We want to keep him. While he is in your program, I will keep his job open part-time on weekends.

I am glad to talk with the committee about him. You can reach me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager, Hollis Dairy
555-0187
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:
- **His last name:** I only had "Tomás," so add his full name in the first paragraph.
- **No date:** I didn't put a date on it. Add one when you upload it through the portal before February 1.
- **"Fell ill":** You said his father "got sick," and I didn't make it sound any more serious than that. Change the wording if you want to say more.
- **One sentence is my wording, not your facts:** "I expect the written coursework to take him more effort… I also expect him to put that effort in." It's a judgment based on what you told me. Keep it only if you agree with it.
